addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - API usage, tool use, Anthropic SDK usage. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- qemu-runner: Use this agent when you need to run a RISC-V ELF binary through Andes QEMU and get its output. Always use this agent instead of running QEMU directly, as it handles the semihosting fd 9 output capture quirk in Claude Code's sandbox.

Examples:

- assistant: *builds a test binary*
  assistant: "Let me use the qemu-runner agent to execute the binary and check the output"

- user: "Run this ELF at VLEN=512"
  assistant: "I'll use the qemu-runner agent to run it" (Tools: Bash, Read) (Tools: Bash)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

index 369f624..66e3331 100644
--- a/Makefile

@@ -4,13 +4,13 @@
 # Demos that run on every andesim mode (fast / cycle / hybrid).
 SUBDIRS := demo/hello demo/lm demo/lm_slave demo/lm_dma \
            demo/hvm_slave demo/hvm_dma demo/rvv demo/syscall \
-           demo/coremark demo/dhrystone
+           demo/coremark demo/dhrystone demo/memsize
 
 RUN_TARGETS := $(patsubst demo/%,run-%,$(SUBDIRS))
 
 # RUN_TARGETS are deliberately NOT .PHONY: make never matches pattern
 # rules (run-%) against .PHONY targets.
-.PHONY: all run clean $(SUBDIRS)
+.PHONY: all run check clean $(SUBDIRS)
 
 all: $(SUBDIRS)
 
@@ -53,5 +53,37 @@ coremark-%:
 dhrystone-%:
 	$(MAKE) -C demo/dhrystone $@
 
+memsize-%:
+	$(MAKE) -C demo/memsize $@
+
+# Aggregate check: every demo that defines its own `check` runs it (real
+# asserts); the rest are asserted to `run` cleanly (exit 0) across all modes.
+# Continues past failures and reports a summary. Heavy -- coremark/dhrystone
+# run their full cycle/hybrid legs. For one demo use `make check-<name>`.
+check:
+	@fail=""; \
+	for dir in $(SUBDIRS); do \
+	  echo "########## $$dir ##########"; \
+	  if $(MAKE) -C $$dir -n check >/dev/null 2>&1; then \
+	    $(MAKE) -C $$dir check || fail="$$fail $$dir"; \
+	  elif $(MAKE) -C $$dir run; then \
+	    echo "[PASS] $$dir: run exits 0 (no asserts)"; \
+	  else \
+	    echo "[FAIL] $$dir: run failed"; fail="$$fail $$dir"; \
+	  fi; \
+	done; \
+	echo "===================================="; \
+	if [ -z "$$fail" ]; then echo "ALL DEMOS OK"; \
+	else echo "FAILED DEMOS:$$fail"; exit 1; fi
+
+# Single demo: its own `check` if defined, else assert `run` exits 0.
+check-%:
+	@if $(MAKE) -C demo/$* -n check >/dev/null 2>&1; then \
+	  $(MAKE) -C demo/$* check; \
+	else \
+	  echo "demo/$*: no asserts -- running to assert exit 0"; \
+	  $(MAKE) -C demo/$* run; \
+	fi
+
 clean:
 	@for dir in $(SUBDIRS); do $(MAKE) -C $$dir clean; done

# memsize -- one ELF, various `--mem-size`

Shows how `andesim --mem-size` behaves across sizes, boundaries, and bad input.
The payload (`main.c`) verifies a 4 KiB working set, so the checksum is the
same at every size and in every mode -- `--mem-size` sizes the *machine*, not
the result.

## `--mem-size` contract (one flag, per-mode meaning)

| mode   | what `--mem-size` does                                             |
|--------|-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| fast   | forwarded to QEMU `-m`; whole MiB only; QEMU's own 16 GiB ceiling |
| cycle  | validated, then ignored (the engine models its full DRAM window)  |
| hybrid | sizes the shared mmap = guest RAM; capped at 2 GiB - 1 V-scratch page |

Parsing is shared: `<number>[K|M|G|T]`, decimals allowed (`1.5G`), `> 0`.

## Targets

    make all        # build memsize.elf (+ memsize_big.elf, memsize.dump)
    make run        # same ELF on fast, cycle, hybrid-marker, hybrid-pc (MEM=256M)
    make MEM=1G run # override the size
    make sizes      # the SAME fast ELF at 64M / 256M / 1G / 1.5G
    make boundary   # 2047M accepted (largest whole MiB) vs 2G rejected
    make fit        # big ELF: 32M too small (rejected) vs 128M fits
    make negative   # 0 / -5 / abc / 1000 all rejected at parse
    make check      # self-asserting harness: 12 asserts, exit 0 on all-pass

## Boundary (hybrid)

The hybrid window is the 2 GiB AE350 DRAM window minus one 4 KiB V-transport
scratch page reserved on top, so `2047M` is the largest whole-MiB size that
fits and `2G` is rejected -- before any mmap file is allocated.

## Fit: `--mem-size` vs the program's own footprint

`memsize_big.elf` reserves a 64 MiB static array, pushing its static-image top
to ~65 MiB. Ask for less (`--mem-size 32M`) and the driver rejects it *before
any guest code runs* (a static check, not a runtime fault); `128M` fits. This
is the only way the demo makes `--mem-size` change program-level behavior
without faulting.

## Why bash asserts, not gtest

Pass/fail here is an *exit code plus a stdout marker* -- the guest exits via
SimControl, the driver exits with its own code. `check.sh` asserts both in
portable bash, same as andesim's `tests/andes_sim/*.sh`. gtest would mean
cross-compiling libstdc++ + a heap onto the target for no added signal; the
driver's own C++ unit tests already use doctest on the host.

1	/* memsize demo: ONE ELF, run under various --mem-size.
2	 *
3	 * The payload verifies a small working set (4 KiB), so it runs unchanged on
4	 * fast, cycle AND hybrid, at ANY valid --mem-size -- the checksum never depends
5	 * on how much RAM the driver hands out.
6	 *
7	 * FOOTPRINT_MB (default 0) reserves a large static .bss array. The "big" build
8	 * (-DFOOTPRINT_MB=64) pushes the ELF's static-image top past a small --mem-size,
9	 * so the driver rejects it BEFORE any guest code runs (a pure driver check, not
10	 * a runtime fault). That is how --mem-size becomes observable in program terms;
11	 * see the Makefile `fit` / `check` targets.
12	 *
13	 * ROI markers are RISC-V HINT NOPs, so the same binary also runs standalone on
14	 * silicon; pc-trigger names the same window as `work` .. memsize_roi_end.
15	 */
16	#include <stdint.h>
17	#include <stdio.h>
18	
19	#include <andesim/ROI.h>
20	
21	#ifndef FOOTPRINT_MB
22	#define FOOTPRINT_MB 0
23	#endif
24	#if FOOTPRINT_MB > 0
